170.founded_by: net-fishing families of the southern shore
170.history: A landing of drying-racks and boat-sheds on the southern coast, Baile ghorm grew through the Holy Age into the largest harbour between the capital and the eastern capes. Its people keep the order of the Stone, whose stone is Clach, and its quays are lined with the wolf-head posts, for the wolf of the Fianna, that mark a harbour of that order. Since the Long War it has been the station of An treas cabhlach, the third fleet, and its yards do more repair work for the crown than fishing for themselves. Its smaller twin, Baile dhomhain, lies a short walk inland and sends it timber and rope.
170.known_for: the third fleet's anchorage and wolf-post quays

171.founded_by: millers of the house of Tormod mac Ruairidh
171.history: A long mill-race cut beside a south-eastern stream gave the town its name and its living, grinding the grain of the farms about the other Baile ghorm. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the roads past Làrach an Dùin carried ore-wagons and the thieves who followed them. It keeps the Old Spirits, and the millers still leave the first sack of each season at the race-head for the ancestors. Cnoc bhàn on the hill above buys most of its flour.
171.known_for: the long mill-race and first-sack offering

172.history: The name promises a great town and the place has never been one; the chroniclers suppose it was large only beside the shielings around it when it was named. It is a quiet market for wool from the moor, dependent on Cnoc dhubh for its road and on Tobar fhiadhaich for its law. Its folk follow the druid schools of the Old Faith and keep a small reading-house where the druid schools' questions are argued on winter nights.
172.known_for: moorland wool and an ill-fitting name

173.history: A low well in a hollow below Muileann shean, ringed with stone in the Holy Age and watched ever since. The small keep that gives it a citadel was built to guard the water for the mill town in dry years, and the dry summers since have proved the builders right. It remains a village, owned in all but name by the millers upstream.

174.founded_by: Ròdaich ford-wardens, resettled by the Tuathaich
174.history: A long ford on the north-western roads, held by a Ròdaich warden-family through the quiet centuries of the Sundering. After the Severance its houses were emptied and given to Tuathaich families shepherded north, who raised the present walls and made it one of the chief towns of their homeland. The Tuathaich here keep the faith of the Church, and their church stands among the shrines the Ròdaich left behind; the ford is still paid for in toll. Its dubhan works, the largest in the north-west, is now its chief trade, and it binds books, a craft the Tuathaich learned at Muileann leathan.
174.known_for: the long ford and its toll

175.history: The deep ford here could only be crossed on horseback, and a family of ferrymen became a family of lords by owning the one safe path over it. The citadel on the near bank was fought for in the troubles before the Severance and has been the seat of Siorrachd Àth dhomhain since. The town is large and orderly, a house of the druid schools stands by the gate, and Cnoc mhòr and Baile gheal send it their grain.
175.known_for: the horseman's ford and shire citadel

176.founded_by: Ròdaich salt-boilers, resettled by the Tuathaich
176.history: A white-washed Ròdaich village of the Holy Age, it was one of the settlements emptied and handed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers made it a town and a market, trading with the harbour at Caol naomh a short distance away. Its church stands in the shell of the older Ròdaich shrine of Manannan, and the two sets of carvings can still be told apart.
176.known_for: the church in the old shrine

177.history: Rough ground behind the river port of Inis bheag, broken to the plough in the long centuries after the Sundering fleet had gone. It feeds the river port and its fishing boats, and it has grown larger than many towns while keeping the name and customs of a village. The druid schools have a strong following among its farmers, who are said to argue the schools' questions over the furrow.
177.known_for: stony fields that feed Inis bheag

178.founded_by: shepherds of the Cuan ghlas hills
178.history: A damp hill-town above the river port of Cuan ghlas, its name taken from the mists that sit on it most mornings. It was never walled and never fought over, and its people send wool and cheese down to the river quays and to Cnoc chiar. A small house of the druid schools keeps the only books in the place.

179.founded_by: boatmen of the Baile Mòr dhomhain river
179.history: The old ford and landing that served Baile Mòr dhomhain before the city had quays of its own. Barges from the landing carry the city's goods to the coast, and the boatmen's guild here is older than the city's walls. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith like its great neighbour and is counted, for most purposes, as the city's river-port.
179.known_for: the river landing of Baile Mòr dhomhain

180.history: A small city on a headland over a deep reach of the Abhainn naomh, with a citadel that looks down the river toward the sea and back toward the mountain roads. River boats put in here with the cargoes landed at Ceann mhin, at the river mouth, for the library town of Muileann chaol, whose scholars and copyists travel through its gate, and its quay-masters have long kept a copy of every cargo list for the Leabharlann. The druid schools hold the city, and its scholars are counted among the library's oldest correspondents.
180.known_for: the library's river landing and cargo registers

181.history: A red-banked ford where the drovers' road crosses a stream in the east, it has been a cattle-market since the Holy Age. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and the drovers still pour a cup into the ford before driving a herd across. The town trades beasts to Seann Dunn on the coast and hides to Baile shean. Furs and hides from the eastern hills are sold at its fair.
181.known_for: the drovers' ford and cattle fair

182.history: A ford over grey water on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the south, it grew up around a quarry whose pale-grey stone faces half the city's houses. The quarry is now worked out, and the town has shrunk to a waystation for carriers. Its people keep to the druid schools of the Old Faith.

183.history: A pale hill in the midlands, crowned by a house of Òrd Mhacha, the order of the capital. The town grew around the druids' farms and remains a quiet place of tithe-barns and schools that train acolytes for the capital's temples of Macha. Baile dhomhain and Àth ghlas send it their tithes and their sons.

184.history: A crooked hill-town raised when the extraction contracts pushed the diggings out from the central mountains toward the coast. Its walls were thrown up against the raids of the troubles before the war, and the shafts beneath it gave out before the Severance. It is now a small town of the druid schools that sends its young to the river port at Ros fhionn.
184.known_for: abandoned shafts beneath a walled hill

185.founded_by: the millers of the wide stream
185.history: A broad mill on a slow river, old enough that its founding is recorded only in the king-lists of the Holy Age. It grinds for the coast-town of Seann Mhorn and for the villages round Àth àrsaidh, and its people keep the Old Spirits. The temple ruins of Làrach an Teampaill lie in the hills behind it, and the millers will not quarry them.
185.known_for: wide mill-wheels, grain for Seann Mhorn

186.history: The Seann-Dhaoine left the harbour-stones and the name Morn; the Ròdaich, finding both, called the place Seann Mhorn and built on top. It is a walled port with a citadel over the harbour mouth, fought over more than once in the troubles before the Severance, and it keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich. Stones of the older builders are set into the harbour wall, and the fishermen touch one before they sail.
186.known_for: Seann-Dhaoine stones in the harbour wall

187.history: A walled town on a bend of the road below Cathair mhòr, raised to store and guard the tithe-grain of the Doire mhin country. Its walls were strengthened when the human administration raised the tithe, and the chroniclers note that the grain was guarded but not shared. It keeps the order of Macha and serves Cill fhada and Muileann ruadh as their market. The dubhan works under its walls supply the forges of the gulf, and the town boils soap.

188.history: A small mill-town built of red sandstone, grinding for Baile chrom and the village of Cill fhada. It was never walled, relying on Baile chrom's walls in hard times. Its people keep the order of Macha, and the mill-house has a small shrine to Macha's black horse above the wheel.

189.history: The lesser of the two Baile chroms in the central midlands, this one lies under the citadel of Dùn chrom and grew as its stockyard. The fighting at Muileann ghlas in the last year of the Long War passed close enough that the town housed wounded for a season. It keeps the order of Macha.

190.founded_by: fishing clans of the southern shore
190.history: A red-cliffed harbour on the southern coast that was a fishing town for three ages. The Great Wave, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, struck it in a single night in the first years of the new kingdom and destroyed the lower town with its fleet, and the harbour was rebuilt higher up the cliff. Its people keep the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and every house facing the sea keeps a lamp in the upper window. The harbour is on Eilean bhàn, the largest island off the south coast, which it shares with Cnoc chaol.

191.history: A harbour on a wild strait whose pilots earned their living guiding ships through the rocks. It is the seat of Siorrachd Caol fhiadhaich and a large town of the order of the Stone, trading with the great tavern-village of Doire shean on its road. The strait pilots still take no ship through without an offering to Clach, the Stone, at the harbour wolf-stone.

192.founded_by: unknown builders, later the Ròdaich keepers of the Old Spirits
192.history: The holy city of the north grew around a ring of stones older than the Ròdaich, and the chroniclers do not claim to know who raised them. The Ròdaich made it a place of the Old Spirits in the Holy Age and it has never had walls, since the ancestors' ground was held to need none. It is a city of pilgrims and hostels, and the spirit-house keepers of Cnoc chiar and Inis bheag answer to its elders. Dubhan from the works below the town and books copied in its hostels are its trades; the elders have never blessed the works, since dubhan is not of the vein.
192.known_for: the unwalled ring of the ancestors

193.history: A white town named for the lime-kilns that whitened it, walled in the Age of Strangers after raids on the road to the harbour at Inis naomh. It is paired with Cnoc mhòr on the hill above, and the two share a market and a quarrel over which is older. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith.

194.history: A town of fulling-mills and white cloth between the port-city of Ros chiar and the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach. Its fullers bleached wool for the harbours of the north coast and still do, though in smaller measure since the trade moved to Inis mhòr. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

195.founded_by: the ford-wardens of Baile Mòr dhomhain
195.history: One of the island's many narrow fords, this one a walled post on the north road into Baile Mòr dhomhain. The city built its walls to hold the crossing in the troubles before the Severance, and it is still garrisoned in name. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
195.known_for: walled ford on the city's north road

196.history: The smaller and older of the two Muileann chaols, a narrow mill beside a small keep in the eastern hills. The great library stands in its namesake to the south-east, and the library's carriers are said still to bring misaddressed parcels here. It is a town of the druid schools, and its mill feeds the villages of Achadh gharbh and Tobar dhubh.

197.history: An old river port on the narrows of the Abhainn ìseal, above its meeting with the Abhainn chaol, and one of the great river ports of the island, seat of Siorrachd Caol shean. It sent the ore of the central mountains down the river to Seann Mhorn when the extraction was at its height, and now sends dubhan and grain the same way. The spring of Allt an Àigh lies in its hinterland, and pilgrims to it come up the river and land here; the town follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
197.known_for: the great eastern river port, pilgrims' landing

198.history: A black hill where charcoal burners worked through the long centuries of the Sundering, the Small-Burning Law forbidding them the ore. It is the largest of the cluster of Cnocs in the eastern hills and their common market. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its charcoal is still sold to smiths who will not work with dubhan.

199.history: The 'young hill' was settled by families spilling out of Cnoc dhubh when the mass excavation drew workers to the eastern hills. It has little of its own beyond houses and a meeting-hall of the druid schools, and its people work in the fields and shops of its larger neighbour.

200.history: A low harbour on the western coast, sheltered by Ros bheag, which it has always served as a lesser port. Its people follow the order of Manannan, the order that runs along the west. The fighting of the Long War at Àth leathan was near enough that the harbour carried supplies for the crown's regiments.

201.history: A long oak grove east of the capital cut for ship-timber since the Holy Age, and the shipwrights who built the Sundering fleet are said to have taken their keels here. The village grew enormous without changing its name, and it is now the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhada and a river port of the capital's order, Macha's, on the Abhainn fhionn. The grove itself is mostly gone, and the village keeps one old oak fenced by the river quay.

202.founded_by: the millers of the deep race
202.history: A mill on a deep, fast race in the central country and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann dhomhain. It was a milling town for centuries and grew rich carrying grain to the mining settlements in the Age of Strangers, when the camps could no longer feed themselves. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and its grain-exchange still sets the price of flour for the south-east.

203.founded_by: the tavern-keepers of the white headland
203.history: A walled river port on a pale headland where the Abhainn gheal meets the Abhainn bhàn, with the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às at its gate, where travellers eat dried venison. It grew around the tavern road, and its walls went up in the troubles, when the roadside houses became militia posts. It keeps the Old Spirits, trades with the great village of Achadh mhòr close by, and sends its goods down the Abhainn bhàn to Seann Warr on the coast.
203.known_for: An Sligeanach Fad' às and dried venison

204.founded_by: the lords of the western plain
204.history: A great fair walled city of the west, seat of lords before the kingdom and a fortress since. Its citadel was held by Ròdaich forces through the war that ended in the Severance, and it is a city of the order of the Stone. It is the chief market of the plain between the capital and the western harbours. Its own vineyards give the plain's wine, and the town salts meat, makes boots and dips candles.
204.known_for: the fair citadel of the western plain

205.history: A holy strait-harbour near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where the orthodox order of Brìde's flame built a landing for pilgrims coming to the mountain of Crom's stone. It is one of the few towns where Òrd Bhrìde holds the majority, and its druids were among those who formalized the order's rite in the first years of the new kingdom. It is a small town and quiet outside the pilgrim season. Pilgrims' boats from the southern Seann Skell come round to its landing by Slighe-mhara chritheanach, the shaking sea-way, named for the swell off the south cape.

206.history: A low field village in the south-east, farming for the mill town of Muileann dhomhain and the port of Ceann chaol. It keeps the Old Spirits and has no history the chroniclers found worth writing beyond its harvests.

207.history: A fair ford in the north below the city of Dùn thais, on the road from the Seann-Dhaoine harbour at Seann Bhrenn. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich and remains a small crossing town.

208.founded_by: the strait-watchers of the north coast
208.history: A small harbour-village on the northern strait, with a citadel built to watch the channel. It served Baile Mòr mhòr as a signal-station and watch-post and has never outgrown that role. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and the watch-fire on its citadel is still lit on the old feast nights.

209.founded_by: Ròdaich oak-cutters, resettled by the Tuathaich
209.history: A small Ròdaich village in a grey oak grove until the Severance, when the families shepherded north were gathered here before being sent on, and so many stayed that it became the largest settlement in the Tuathaich homeland almost at once. It never took a town's name, and the Tuathaich keep it a village in speech on purpose. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire ghlas and the heart of the Tuathaich Church, whose priests are said to hold the oldest copy of the voyage of Naomh Breandan here; the library has asked to copy it and been refused. Its wool mills, built with the Moot's money, make the grey twill of the north.

210.founded_by: the peat-cutters of the northern moor
210.history: A black hill of peat in the north, cut for fuel since the Small-Burning Law left the ore to the custodians and ordinary hearths to turf. It is the road-town for Baile mhòr and Àth shean and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. The peat-banks are now nearly as worked out as the vein.
210.known_for: peat cut from the black hill

211.history: A dusky hill beside the harbour of Seann Toll, settled by keepers of the Old Spirits who tended waymarks on the pilgrim road to Cathair naomh. It remains a small town of hostels and way-shrines, busy in the feast seasons and empty between them.

212.founded_by: the first millers of the northern river
212.history: The old mill of the north, whose wheel the Holy Age king-lists already call ancient, and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann shean. Its walls went up in the Age of Strangers, when it ground grain for the mining camps on contract and was raided for it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and owns the well-village of Tobar ìseal below it.
212.known_for: the oldest mill-wheel in the north

213.founded_by: Ròdaich millers of the Seann Skell country
213.history: A crooked mill on the edge of the north-west, left in Ròdaich hands when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed around it. It keeps the order of Manannan, whose sea-feasts its Tuathaich neighbours keep beside their church's, and its millers have ground for both peoples since the Severance, which the chroniclers note without comment. Cnoc ghlas and Àth àrsaidh over the line buy its flour.
213.known_for: a Ròdaich mill on the Tuathaich line

214.founded_by: hill-farmers of the Àth dhomhain country
214.history: The great hill above Baile gheal, farmed since the Holy Age and never walled, since Baile gheal's walls stand close below. The two towns share a market and a long quarrel over which is the elder. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
214.known_for: hill farms and a quarrel with Baile gheal

215.history: A dusky headland city on the north coast, walled, with a citadel on the rock and a harbour below. It was one of the harbours the human traders first used after the Crossing, and its citadel was taken and retaken in the war before the Severance. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and competes with Caol bheag for the northern trade. Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast to Caol mhin, begins at its harbour; the grain barges of Inis mhòr sailed it until the roads took their trade.

216.founded_by: Ròdaich shrine-keepers, resettled by the Tuathaich
216.history: A low church-site village of the Ròdaich, emptied at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families. It has grown past any village size, with its church at its heart, and it farms for the harbour of Ros ruadh. The Tuathaich here call it by its Ròdaich name and no other.

217.founded_by: Ròdaich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich
217.history: A pale hill with a citadel built by a Ròdaich family in the Holy Age, taken over by the Tuathaich when their homeland was fixed. The Tuathaich garrison it as a guard-post on their southern marches, and it follows the faith of the Church. The town sells cattle and hides to Cnoc àrsaidh.

218.founded_by: the ford-guards of Baile Mòr dhomhain
218.history: A dusky ford on the west road out of Baile Mòr dhomhain, walled against the roads' thieves in the Age of Strangers. It is a carriers' town, and the road-house An Taigh-seinnse Reòta at Muileann fhada lies a short way down the road. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
218.known_for: carriers' town on the west road

219.history: A narrow ford in the east where the road to the harbour at Inis mhin crosses a stream. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and its ford runs low in the dry months. It is a small market town for the holy field of Achadh naomh.
219.known_for: narrow ford on the Inis mhin road

220.history: A small walled hill in the east, raised as a refuge for the herds of Achadh naomh in the troubled years. Its pastures are thin, and the town has always kept fewer herds than its walls could shelter. It keeps the Old Spirits.

221.history: A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway, walled, with a small harbour. The seal-hunters who settled it in the Holy Age became traders and then wall-builders, since the eastern waters were a haunt of pirates in the Age of Strangers. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the harbour for Àth chaol and Achadh naomh.

222.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers of the west coast
222.history: A wild field village on the far western shore with a small harbour, kept in Ròdaich hands when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed to the north. It faces the waters where the Sea-Watcher is said to live, and pirates are still seen off the coast. Its people follow the order of Manannan.
222.known_for: fishing within sight of the Sea-Watcher's waters

223.founded_by: the river-lords of the Abhainn ìseal
223.history: An ancient river port a little below Cuan bheag on the Abhainn ìseal, trading grain from the fields around Baile fhiadhaich since the Holy Age. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Its stone jetty is held to be the oldest on the island still in use, and it is patched each generation rather than rebuilt.

224.history: A small town in a deep valley, farming for the druids of Macha at Cnoc bhàn. It has no walls and little history beyond the tithe-rolls of the druids' house, which record its harvests without a gap from the Sundering to the present.
224.known_for: tithe-fields of the Cnoc bhàn druids

225.history: A narrow harbour ford in the far east, close to the old Seann-Dhaoine harbour of Seann Tarr. It keeps the Old Spirits and sends its fishing to the market at Cnoc uaine.

226.history: A young town in the eastern hills close by the ruins of Làrach an Teampaill, whose altar faces the vein. Its early houses were built of stones carried off the ruins, a use the elders of the Old Spirits later forbade. It keeps the Old Spirits and serves travellers who come to look at the ruins.
226.known_for: houses of stone from Làrach an Teampaill

227.history: An ancient ford in the east, between the mill town of Muileann leathan and Seann Mhorn on the coast. It keeps the Old Spirits and a ford-stone where travellers leave a pebble, and it has been a small crossing town since the Holy Age.

228.history: A narrow ford-town in the central hills, grown in the Age of Strangers around the camp-roads to the diggings near Cill ghlas. The Rending, Scàineadh Cill ghlas, killed miners of this town in the collapse, and the people here still use scàinte of a man who is shaken. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

229.history: A red walled mill town beside Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, the hot springs whose warm water drives its wheel through winter. The springs were held sacred by the Old Spirits, and the healers of the Old Faith call them Dian Cècht's, and the town walled them against claims from the human administration. It is a place for the sick and the old to bathe.
229.known_for: the hot springs of Muileann ruadh

230.history: A white oak grove between Seann Dunn and Seann Mhorn, cut for charcoal and ship-timber. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a large, quiet village with no walls.

231.history: A holy city near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, built by the druids of Macha in the Holy Age as a seat of learning. The ruins are said to have been older than any Ròdaich memory when the city was founded, and the druids left them as they were. It is unwalled and trades with the harbour of Seann Chwen and with Ceann leathan.
231.known_for: the druids' city by the old outpost

232.founded_by: the white-cloth weavers of the west
232.history: A large white town of the western plain and the seat of Siorrachd Baile gheal. It is a city of the order of the Stone in all but name, and it trades cloth with Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbour of Inis thais.
232.known_for: white cloth of the western plain

233.history: A walled pale hill in the south-east above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, which grinds its grain. The walls were raised when the road from Làrach an Dùin became unsafe. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the market of the southern-eastern farms. It sends the pearls of the south-eastern shallows and the clay of its fields to other markets.

234.founded_by: Ròdaich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich
234.history: A wide mill on a northern stream, walled with a citadel, and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann leathan. It was a Ròdaich town until the Severance, when the Tuathaich took it over as one of the principal towns of their homeland. It is a centre of the Tuathaich Church, and its keep is where the Tuathaich northern coast is governed.

235.founded_by: Ròdaich green-dyers, resettled by the Tuathaich
235.history: A green-grey town of dyers, emptied at the Severance and resettled by the Tuathaich. It keeps the Tuathaich Church and is a market for Baile Mòr ruadh and Cnoc ghlas.
235.known_for: green dyes and Tuathaich church feasts

236.founded_by: Ròdaich shore-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich
236.history: An ancient walled town near the harbour of Caol mhòr, one of the Ròdaich towns resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The walls are older than the Ròdaich say they know, and the Tuathaich have kept them. It follows the faith of the Church.
236.known_for: old walls in the Tuathaich north

237.history: A small walled harbour on a tidal islet of the north coast, near the holy city of Cathair naomh. It ferries pilgrims from the sea to the holy city and keeps the Old Spirits.
237.known_for: the pilgrims' ferry to Cathair naomh

238.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich
238.history: A red headland harbour on the north-west coast, one of the Ròdaich harbours given to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The fishing families of Ros ruadh are among those who keep the voyage of Naomh Breandan alive in speech, and some say the saint's boat put out from this headland. It follows the faith of the Church.
238.known_for: the Naomh Breandan telling of the north-west

239.history: A smooth headland port, walled, and the seat of Siorrachd Ceann mhin. It was a trading harbour for the northern mines in the Age of Strangers and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Slighe Ceann mhin, the long road down the east of the island to Seann Dunn, begins at its gate.

240.history: A small mill that grew into a sizable town and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann bheag. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and grinds for the harbour at Ros chiar. It shares its name with three others on the island, including the Tuathaich lighthouse town.

241.history: A red town of the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile ruadh. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades grain with Achadh naomh.

242.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich
242.history: An ancient field village on the far western coast, facing the waters of Uilebheist na Mara, the Sea-Watcher. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, struck it in the Age of Strangers; it was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and keeps the faith of the Church. Pirates have been seen offshore and the villagers keep watch on the headland. Its boats first met the humans' ships at sea, off the north-west cape at the place they call Coinneachadh nan Long.

243.history: A dusky hill near the standing stone Colbh Cnoc chiar, which carries only the words Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire'. The stone was old when the Ròdaich came, and the town grew around the families who tended it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose druids still come to argue over the imperative that no one has explained.

244.founded_by: Ròdaich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich
244.history: An ancient mill town of the north-west, and seat of Siorrachd Muileann àrsaidh, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A second Muileann àrsaidh lies close by, and the two are called the elder and the younger. It follows the faith of the Church.
244.known_for: the elder of the two ancient mills

245.founded_by: druids of the order of Manannan
245.history: A holy oak grove in the west near Àth leathan, where the Long War's first battle was fought. It stayed Ròdaich and kept the order of Manannan, and it buried many of the dead of that battle in its grove. The grove is closed to strangers.
245.known_for: graves of the Àth leathan dead

246.history: A narrow mill town in the eastern hills, and the home of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the library that keeps the most complete record of the island. The library was founded in the new kingdom and has since taken in the provincial archives, and its war archive is sealed. The town lives on the library and on the river landing at Ceann dhomhain, and to put a thing in the Library is to settle it. Paper has been made here since the Age of Sundering, and its copyists and binders work for the library.
246.known_for: Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the great library

247.founded_by: druids of the order of Manannan
247.history: A holy mill in the west, the seat of Siorrachd Muileann naomh, whose wheel is said to have been consecrated to Manannan mac Lir. It lies near the Àth leathan battlefield and was taken over by crown regiments in the Long War. It follows the order of Manannan.

248.history: A small ford in the west on the road between Baile fhiadhaich and Cnoc ìseal. It follows the order of Manannan and has never been much more than a crossing, though crown regiments marched through it to Àth leathan in the Long War.

249.history: A harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the eastern coast, named Seann Tarr by the Ròdaich, and the seat of the shire of the same name. It is a large village that follows the Old Spirits. The eastern pirates made it unsafe in the Age of Strangers, and it has a small fleet of its own.
249.known_for: the old eastern harbour and fleet

250.history: A hill-city with a citadel close to the capital, raised by lords of the Doire mhin country who held the roads north of Cathair dhearg. It has always been a garrison town and was one of the strongholds from which the war before the Severance was fought. It follows the order of Macha and draws on the tithe-granaries of Baile chrom and the great village of Doire mhin. It is not the Cathair mhòr of the third regiment, which lies further east. Its glass-house is the largest on the island.
250.known_for: the citadel on the capital's north road

251.history: A temple-site village strung along a long ridge near Baile chrom, whose temple of Macha is the longest building in the district. It farms for the market at Baile chrom and sends its grain to the tithe-granaries there.

252.history: A young hill-town with a citadel beside the silver mine of Muileann chiar, raised when the Ròdaich held the silver seam against the human claims. The citadel was built to guard the seam, and the town grew as the silver town expanded. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
252.known_for: the citadel over the silver seam

253.history: A low well-village in the east that waters the city of Dùn dhearg in dry seasons. It keeps the Old Spirits, and its well-keepers still bless the water before it is carted up the hill.
253.known_for: the well that waters Dùn dhearg

254.founded_by: red-clay potters of the Cuan shean country
254.history: A red town of potters and brick-makers behind the harbour of Cuan shean, whose kilns have fired the roof-tiles of the western coast since the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the order of Manannan, and its potters mark each jar with a small scorpion, the order's badge, under the base. Most of what it makes goes out through Cuan shean.

255.founded_by: the lords of the bent hill
255.history: A fortified city on a crooked hill in the midlands, seat of Siorrachd Dùn chrom, with a citadel that commands the roads south of the capital. The last battle of the Long War, at Muileann ghlas, was fought within sight of its citadel, and the crown's commanders used its citadel as their headquarters. It follows the order of Macha and is served by the stockyard town of Baile chrom and the ford at Àth mhin.

256.history: A dusky ford in the south-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Àth chiar and a large market town. Its keep was held by Ròdaich rebels in the war before the Severance and is still garrisoned. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the coast at Seann Mhorn and Muileann chiar to the south.
256.known_for: the rebels' keep and southern cattle-market

257.history: The deep town a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, where the harbour's rope-walks and timber-yards were moved to be clear of storms. The panthers' migration road, Imrich nam Pantar, crosses its fields, and the townsfolk shut their stock in when the cats pass. It follows the order of the Stone and works almost entirely for the harbour and its fleet.

258.history: A red ford-town near the north-east coast, whose name was given to Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, one of the five lighthouses built in the Age of Strangers at the request of human navigators. The beacon burned the ore for more than a century and was among the first things on the island converted to dubhan. The town keeps the Old Spirits and lives by the coast road and the lighthouse.
258.known_for: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, the north-east beacon

259.founded_by: Ròdaich farmers of the red ground
259.history: A red town in the north-west that stayed Ròdaich when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed around it, and the line of the border wall that was proposed and never built would have run past its gate. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and its market is used by Tuathaich from Baile fhionn and Ròdaich from Àth uaine alike.
259.known_for: a shared market on the border

260.founded_by: Ròdaich headland-fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich
260.history: A black headland harbour on the north-west coast, all but joined to the city of Inis àrsaidh. It was a Ròdaich fishing town until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich harbour since. It follows the faith of the Church, and its boats sail with Inis àrsaidh's.
260.known_for: the black headland beside Inis àrsaidh

261.founded_by: the oak-keepers of the Old Spirits
261.history: A fair oak grove in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhionn and a large village of the Old Spirits. The grove has never been cut for ship-timber, its keepers holding it for the ancestors, and it lies on the road between Cathair naomh and the Tuathaich line.
261.known_for: an uncut grove of the ancestors

262.history: A white hill in the north-east, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc gheal, looking down on the Seann-Dhaoine harbour of Seann Bhrenn. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is the market for Baile dhìreach and Àth dhearg.
262.known_for: the white hill market of the north-east

263.founded_by: Ròdaich herders, resettled by the Tuathaich
263.history: A small green-grey hill town of the north-west, emptied and resettled at the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and trades with the Ròdaich mill at Muileann chrom over the line.
263.known_for: trade across the line at Muileann chrom

264.history: A straight town on the road from Cnoc gheal to Seann Bhrenn, named for the road that made it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is a carters' stop on the way to the coast.
264.known_for: the straight road to Seann Bhrenn

265.founded_by: the grove-keepers of the Old Spirits
265.history: A green oak grove in the north-east, not the Doire uaine of the Hollow Man's hills, a confusion the library records note with some weariness. It keeps the Old Spirits and cuts its oak for Muileann bheag.

266.history: A red mill town beside Muileann fhada in the north-east, the two together grinding for Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

267.history: An ancient cell-site village in the north-east, older than the druid schools that now hold it. The founding shrine is said to have been of the Old Spirits, and its foundations lie under the present meeting-house. It is a large village supplying Muileann bheag.
267.known_for: a druids' house on an old shrine

268.history: A wild hill above Ceann mhin, settled by hunters and later by carters on the harbour road. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and sends game and hides down to the port.
268.known_for: game and hides for Ceann mhin

269.founded_by: Ròdaich hill-farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich
269.history: A damp hill in the north-west, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc thais, and one of the larger Tuathaich towns since the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and is the market of the two Muileann àrsaidhs.
269.known_for: the market of the two ancient mills

270.history: A grey river port on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan ghlas, and a large village, whose barges go down to Ros chiar at the river mouth. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is served by the hill town of Cnoc thais above it.
270.known_for: the grey river port and its citadel

271.history: A rough field village beside the older Muileann chaol, breaking stony ground for the mill. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and shares its name with two other Achadh gharbhs of the east, which the library's clerks tell apart only by their shires.
271.known_for: stony fields for the old mill

272.history: A young well village in the north-east, dug to water the fields behind Inis bheag when those fields were first broken. It has grown into a sizeable village and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
272.known_for: the young well behind Inis bheag

273.founded_by: the lords of the deep river
273.history: A walled city with a citadel on a deep river in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Baile Mòr dhomhain. It was one of the great market cities of the north through the Holy Age and the Sundering and a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and holds its four fords and its river landing at Àth shean. It is the market town of the northern hills and the second cattle-market of the island. The white marble of its hills is quarried nearby, and the town is known for its books.
273.known_for: the deep-river city and its fords

274.history: A green mill in the wooded middle west, one of the few towns where Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the Hawk order, whose rite is the older form of Òrd Bhrìde's, still holds. The carved hawk over the mill-door is said to be as old as the Binding of the First Flame. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers, and since then the second sense of 'uaine' has clung to its name.

275.history: A small young town on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and Baile Mòr àrsaidh, grown from a carters' stable. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and lives by changing horses.
275.known_for: a carters' stop between two cities

276.history: A large well village in the central-east, laid out along a straight channel that carries its water. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and supplies water and vegetables to Baile Mòr uaine and Baile thais. Its paper-mill makes the paper of the royal chronicle.

277.history: A rough ford on the hill road near Baile Mòr uaine, where the drovers rest their beasts. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is a very small place. Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the spring where the keeper's stone cup was first checked against its copies, lies on the moor between the ford and Tobar dhìreach.
277.known_for: a drovers' ford in the hills

278.history: A deep ford on the road from Caol shean inland, where goods from the river port are loaded from boats to carts. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
278.known_for: the inland ford of Caol shean

279.founded_by: the keepers of Allt an Àigh
279.history: A rough field village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream said to grant fortune to those who drink at the right phase of the moon. Pilgrims have come since the Holy Age, and the keepers' citadel was built to guard the stream from anyone who would bottle and sell it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose druids have never agreed whether the stream's luck is real.
279.known_for: Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune

280.founded_by: hunters of the Muileann chrom country
280.history: A wild walled hill in the middle country, near the canoe-landing of Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine. Its walls were raised in the troubled years when the river road carried ore. It follows the order of Macha and trades with Muileann chrom and Inis ìseal.
280.known_for: a walled hill by the river road

281.history: A blue-grey hill town just north of Cathair mhòr, pasturing the garrison's horses. It follows the order of Macha and has always been the city's stable.

282.founded_by: the harbour-lords of the west coast
282.history: The old harbour of the west, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan shean and one of the largest towns on the island. It shipped western grain and timber through the Holy Age and served the human traders after the Crossing. Since the Long War it has been home to An ceathramh cabhlach, the fourth fleet. It follows the order of Manannan.

283.founded_by: the fishers of the capital's river
283.history: An ancient field village on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name. It is the seat of Siorrachd Achadh àrsaidh, and its river quays land the fish and grain that feed Cathair dhearg. It follows the order of Macha.
283.known_for: the river quays that feed the capital

284.founded_by: farmers of the Seann Chwen country
284.history: A low town in the middle east, a short way south of Cill ghlas and the ground the Rending tore open. It follows the order of Macha and sends its grain to the harbour at Seann Chwen.
284.known_for: grain town south of Cill ghlas

285.founded_by: fishers of the far east coast
285.history: A small low town on the far east coast, beside Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, one of the five lighthouses completed in the Age of Strangers. Pirates are still seen off this coast, and the lighthouse-keepers double as the town's watch. It keeps the Old Spirits.
285.known_for: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and the pirate watch

286.founded_by: druids of the order of Manannan
286.history: A holy ford near Cuan shean, where the druids of Manannan bless the carts that go down to the harbour. It follows the order of Manannan and is a small town of shrine-keepers and carters. Bog-iron is dug in the moss behind the town, and its forges have made arms and field-guns for the regiments since An Cogadh Fada.

287.history: A small dusky hill between Doire mhin and Muileann ruadh, pastured by herders of the great village. It follows the order of Macha.

288.history: A white stone mill in the south-east that grinds for the city of Dùn dhearg. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a large mill-town with a guild of millers older than the city's walls.

289.history: A long hill in the south-east farmed in terraces since the centuries after the Sundering. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with Muileann dhomhain.
289.known_for: terraced farms on the long hill

290.founded_by: the lords of the wild hill
290.history: A small wild city on a hill south of the capital, near Achadh mhin, which the Great Wave struck. Its hill kept it clear of the water, and it took in the survivors of the villages below. It follows the order of Macha. The clay of its hill makes it the largest pottery on Rodos, and Cathair fhada sells its ware to the north.

291.history: A fair field village in the south-east, with meadows between the hill-towns of Cnoc shean and Cnoc fhada. It keeps the Old Spirits and is known for its hay.

292.history: A great hill in the south, above the harbour of Seann Warr and the large mill town of Muileann bhàn. It keeps the Old Spirits, and its hill-farms supply both.

293.founded_by: the lords of the old hill
293.history: A small old hill-town with a citadel in the west, commanding the road between Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbours of the south-west. It follows the order of the Stone and has kept a garrison since the war before the Severance.

294.founded_by: millers of the Seann Bhral country
294.history: A dusky mill town with a citadel in the south-east, not the silver town of the same name further north; the confusion of the two is an old grievance here. It grinds for Àth chiar and the harbour of Seann Bhral. It keeps the Old Spirits.

295.history: The Seann-Dhaoine left the harbour-mole and the name Dunn; the Ròdaich called it Seann Dunn and built a citadel over the mole. It is the seat of the shire of the same name and follows the order of Macha. It is a village in form but large in number, with the ford-town of Àth ghorm under its protection.

296.history: A wild oak grove in the south, grown into a very large village and the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhiadhaich. It follows the order of Macha and supplies timber to the city of Cathair fhada close by.

297.founded_by: the lords of the long city
297.history: A long walled city in the south, strung along a ridge between the capital's country and the coast, and the seat of Siorrachd Cathair fhada. It follows the order of Macha and has always been one of the capital's chief supports. The Fèill Muileann òg is held a short way north, and the city's merchants dominate it. Its market right is among the oldest on the island, and its own trade is in cheese, honey and garments.
297.known_for: merchants of the Fèill Muileann òg

298.history: A blue ford with a small citadel on the road inland from Seann Dunn, built to hold the crossing for the harbour. It follows the order of Macha and is a small town of carters and toll-keepers.

299.history: A rough town on the south coast road between Seann Vell and the lighthouse village of Tobar dhearg. It is one of the few towns where Òrd Bhrìde holds the majority, its orthodox druids having come from the pilgrim harbour at Caol naomh. It trades with Muileann naomh and the great port of Seann Skell.
299.known_for: an orthodox town of Brìde's flame on the coast road

300.history: A green walled hill in the south-west, fortified against pirates who raided the coast in the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the order of the Stone and sends its young to the first fleet at Àth gharbh.

301.history: A small harbour on the northern strait, older than its far larger namesake inland and the one that gave that town its name. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a quiet fishing town, though An ceathramh rèisimeid, stationed at the larger Caol bheag, sends its patrols here. It stands on Eilean fhada, the long island off the north coast, and the strait it is named for is the sound between that island and Rodos.
301.known_for: the elder Caol bheag on the strait

302.history: An old walled ford with a citadel in the north, holding the road between Tobar ghorm and Cnoc dhubh. Its keep was fought for in the war before the Severance. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

303.founded_by: Ròdaich lords, resettled by the Tuathaich
303.history: A red walled city in the north-west, held by Ròdaich lords from the Holy Age to the Severance, and since then one of the principal Tuathaich cities. It follows the faith of the Church and governs the Àth àrsaidh country with its fords and towns.
303.known_for: the red city of the Tuathaich

304.founded_by: Ròdaich ford-keepers, resettled by the Tuathaich
304.history: An ancient ford in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a large town of the Church and the market of the Tuathaich southern country.
304.known_for: the ancient ford of the Tuathaich

305.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich
305.history: A bent town on the far north-west coast, the seat of Siorrachd Baile chrom, beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the first of the five lighthouses in the ring. Since the Severance it has been Tuathaich, and it is the one town where Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the Christian vigil of the Grey Night, holds the majority; its one night of silence is kept for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, takes its name from this town, which it struck in the Age of Strangers. The Church's priests at Ceann mhòr hold that the Grey Night grew out of their own harbour prayer to keep the sea shut, and the bishops call it irregular, the Church gone astray.
305.known_for: the Grey Night vigil and the lighthouse

306.founded_by: Ròdaich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich
306.history: A low walled town in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Baile ìseal, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and is one of the larger Tuathaich towns.
306.known_for: the low walled town of the north-west

307.founded_by: human settlers of the Age of Strangers
307.history: A small white oak grove settled by humans in the early years after the Crossing, one of the few human foundations of the north-west. Its people stayed through the Severance and are among the oldest human families on the island. It follows the faith of the Church.
307.known_for: one of the oldest human families

308.history: A deep well-village in the western hills, dug to supply a mining camp that has since been abandoned. It is one of the smallest villages on the island and follows the order of Manannan. The grassland above the village is where the Leaden Hawk company kept its watch on the road from Ros bheag in the first spring of the Severance war.
308.known_for: the well of a lost camp

309.founded_by: keepers of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
309.history: An old town beside Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people have kept the forest's edge since the Holy Age and keep the Old Spirits, though the forest is now held by the druid schools.
309.known_for: the keepers of the sacred forest's edge

310.history: The 'ancient hill' of the eastern cluster of Cnocs is in fact among the younger of them; the chroniclers think the name was taken from a cairn on its summit rather than from the town. It is a small farming town of the druid schools that sells its barley in Cnoc dhubh and Àth dhomhain.
310.known_for: the summit cairn and eastern barley

311.founded_by: the valley-folk of the eastern narrows
311.history: A town squeezed into a narrow valley in the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile chaol. Its houses climb the valley sides in rows, and the one road through it has been tolled since the Holy Age. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach and the market at Cnoc uaine; the sacred forest of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar lies on its western edge.
311.known_for: terraced houses and the valley toll

312.history: An old well-village in the eastern hills, walled in the troubled years because its well was the only sure water on the road past Làrach an Teampaill. It keeps the Old Spirits, and the well-keepers still close the gate in dry seasons and ration the water by the bucket.
312.known_for: the walled well on the temple road

313.history: A Seann-Dhaoine river port on the Abhainn uaine in the midlands, called Seann Toll by the Ròdaich for the hollow in the rock where its boats lie. It is walled and follows the order of Macha, and it stands a short way west of Cill ghlas, where the Rending opened. It lies close to Ceann leathan at the river mouth, where the Còmhrag is fought each year, and fighters from the tournament fill its taverns.
313.known_for: the rock-hollow landing and Còmhrag crowds

314.founded_by: millers of the Ceann leathan country
314.history: A fair-stoned walled mill town between Ceann leathan and Cuan dhearg, grinding grain landed at Ceann leathan's harbour and Cuan dhearg's river landing. Its walls went up in the Age of Strangers. It follows the order of Macha.

315.founded_by: the custodian house of Dùn ìseal
315.history: A low fort-city in the east with walls, a citadel and a temple, the seat of Siorrachd Dùn ìseal. Its temple is the Hall where Brìde's undying flame was first bound, kept by the Ròdaich custodians through every age; the townsfolk themselves keep the Old Spirits, and their ancestor hall beside it is the chief spirit-house of the eastern hills. It stands between the silver seam of Muileann chiar and the hot springs of Muileann ruadh, and it was held by the Ròdaich in the dispute over the silver. It is the market town of the eastern hills and plain, and the market under the Hall is older than the kingdom. The silver, gold and copper of its hills pass through it as blanks for the mint, and the town salts venison and binds books.

316.founded_by: the oak-keepers of the capital's north
316.history: A smooth-barked oak grove north of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name and customs. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire mhin and follows the order of Macha. Its people farm for Cathair mhòr and send much of their grain to the tithe-granaries at Baile chrom.
316.known_for: the great grove-village of the north road

317.founded_by: ford-keepers of the Seann Chwen country
317.history: A small ford on a bent stream south of Cill ghlas, where the Rending opened. It follows the order of Macha.
317.known_for: bent ford south of Cill ghlas

318.history: A holy hill with a citadel south of the capital, the seat of Siorrachd Cnoc naomh and a house of the order of Macha since the Holy Age. It lies close by the battlefield of Muileann ghlas, and its druids buried the dead of both sides after the Long War's last battle. It is a large town of druids, soldiers and pilgrims.
318.known_for: the druids who buried Muileann ghlas's dead

319.history: A small temple-site village at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest no one has settled or fully mapped. Its temple-house was built to watch the forest rather than enter it. It follows the order of Macha.
319.known_for: the temple-house watching the unclaimed forest

320.history: A small walled town near Cill thais and Baile chiar, west of the capital. The walls were raised in the war before the Severance. It follows the order of Macha and has little trade of its own.

321.history: A young hill town close to Muileann òg, whose fair is the largest gathering on the island. It lodges traders and their beasts during the fair and is quiet the rest of the year. It follows the order of Macha.
321.known_for: lodgings for the Fèill Muileann òg

322.history: A straight hill on the mining road in the south-east, home of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, a famous roadside inn that serves pan-fried spinach with black wine. The inn was fortified as a militia waypoint in the troubles before the Severance and took dubhan lamps with the rest of the tavern circuit. It keeps the Old Spirits and lies close by the ruins of Làrach an Dùin.

323.history: A damp hill above the small harbour of Caol dhomhain in the south-east. It keeps the Old Spirits and sends its cattle to Baile gheal.

324.history: An old oak grove in the south-west, grown into one of the largest villages on the island and the seat of Siorrachd Doire shean. At its heart is Am Buabhall Fortanach, the most famous tavern on the old roads, which serves jugged buffalo and has stood since the Holy Age. It is a harbour as well, where the hulls of the first fleet of Àth gharbh lie, and follows the order of the Stone. Rathad na Banrighinn, Queen Catrìona's stone road from the capital to Inis thais, runs through the village past the tavern.
324.known_for: Am Buabhall Fortanach and jugged buffalo

325.history: A small town on a straight hill road between Caol fhiadhaich and the great mill-town of Muileann bheag. It follows the order of the Stone and is a stop for carters.
325.known_for: carters' stop on the south-west road

326.history: A holy mill in the south, the seat of Siorrachd Muileann naomh, whose druids of the orthodox order of Brìde's flame bless the grain before it is ground. It is one of the few towns of Òrd Bhrìde and trades with Caol ruadh and Seann Skell. Its hawk-house was the southernmost of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the first on Rodos to hang a bronze bell, until it took Òrd Bhrìde's written order in the first years of the restored kingdom; the bell now rings for Brìde's flame.
326.known_for: grain blessed by the druids of Brìde's flame

327.founded_by: Ròdaich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich
327.history: A small mill town on the north coast beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, one of the five lighthouses built in the Age of Strangers. It became Tuathaich at the Severance, and the Tuathaich lighthouse-keepers tended the beacon for the kingdom until it was converted to dubhan. It follows the Tuathaich Church.

328.history: A Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the north coast, called Seann Bhrenn by the Ròdaich, and the seat of the shire of the same name. It is a large village of the Old Spirits, and its fishers tell that the harbour-stones were laid by people who had no need of the Ròdaich's tides.

329.founded_by: Ròdaich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich
329.history: A small fair town in the north-west, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the Tuathaich Church and trades across the line with the Ròdaich town of Baile ruadh.
329.known_for: trade across the line with Baile ruadh

330.founded_by: Ròdaich island-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich
330.history: An ancient island city on the north-west coast, all but joined to Ceann dhubh. It was a Ròdaich harbour-city until the Severance and has been Tuathaich since. It follows the faith of the Church and is one of the few Tuathaich harbours with a fleet of its own.

331.history: A long mill in the north-east beside Muileann dhearg, grinding for the large village of Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

332.history: A dusky headland harbour village on the north-east coast that ships the flour of Muileann bheag. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and competes with Seann Toll for the coast trade.
332.known_for: the flour harbour of Muileann bheag

333.history: A dusky oak grove grown into a large village, the seat of Siorrachd Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its druids are said to hold their disputations under the oldest trees.

334.history: A red town in the east on the road to the harbour at Seann Toll. It keeps the Old Spirits.
334.known_for: red town on the harbour road

335.founded_by: Ròdaich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich
335.history: The younger of the two Muileann àrsaidhs, walled, a short distance from the elder. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, struck it in the Age of Strangers, and it was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church.

336.history: A long field village in the wooded middle west, one of the few settlements where Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the Hawk order, whose rite is the older form of Òrd Bhrìde's, still holds. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. Its fields feed the Hawk-order mill at Muileann uaine.

337.founded_by: Ròdaich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich
337.history: A tiny ancient hill with a citadel, far larger than the handful of people who now live in it. It was a Ròdaich keep until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich watch-post since. It follows the faith of the Church.
337.known_for: an empty citadel on the southern march

338.founded_by: Ròdaich carters of the mining road
338.history: A straight ford with a citadel in the north-east, built as a waystation on the ore road in the Age of Strangers and fortified in the war before the Severance. Since the Long War it has been the station of An dàrna rèisimeid, the second regiment. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.
